rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “they ask you” refers either to Quraysh or the Jews; the famous account has Quraysh asking after Jews prompted them to test Muhammad about the Spirit, the traveler, and the youths.
rows.anchor: الضمير في ويسئلونك عائد على قريش أو على اليهود، والمشهور أن السائلين قريش حين دستها اليهود

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق، وهب
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq identifies Dhū al-Qarnayn as Alexander the Greek; Wahb calls him a Roman. Two views say he was a prophet or a righteous nonprophet; calling him an angel is deemed strange.
rows.anchor: وذو القرنين هو الإسكندر اليوناني ذكره ابن إسحاق. وقال وهب: هو رومي وهل هو نبي أو عبد صالح ليس بنبي قولان

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali reports that Dhū al-Qarnayn was a righteous servant, neither king nor prophet, who died twice after being struck on each horn and was raised each time.
rows.anchor: وعن علي كان عبدا صالحا ليس بملك ولا نبي ضرب على قرنه الأيمن فمات في طاعة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several explanations of his epithet are reported: he reached both ends of the world, had two braids or horns on his crown, lived through two generations, or ruled Romans and Persians; Wahb also describes copper plates on his head.
rows.anchor: وقيل: طاف قرني الدنيا يعني جانبيها شرقها وغربها. وقيل: كان له قرنان أي ضفيرتان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari suggests the name could mark courage, like calling a brave man a ram because he butts his peers; he also says Dhū al-Qarnayn was a Roman, an old woman's only child.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يسمى بذلك لشجاعته كما يسمى الشجاع كبشا كأنه ينطح أقرانه

rows.speaker: أبو الريحان البيروني
rows.claim: Abu Rayhan argues that Dhū al-Qarnayn was the Himyarite Abu Bakr ibn Sammi ibn Umayr ibn Ifriqis, whose realm reached both horizons; he finds this likelier because the Dhu-names belonged to Yemen.
rows.anchor: هو أبو بكر بن سمي بن عمير بن إفريقس الحميري، بلغ ملكه مشارق الأرض ومغاربها

rows.speaker: شاعر من حمير، تبع الحميري
rows.claim: A Himyarite poem praises Dhū al-Qarnayn as a Muslim king who reached east and west; the poem is also attributed to Tubba al-Himyari, supporting the Yemenite identification.
rows.anchor: قد كان ذو القرنين قبلي مسلما ... ملكا علا في الأرض غير مبعد

rows.speaker: علي، ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ali and Ibn Abbas give his name as Abdullah ibn al-Dahhak.
rows.anchor: وعن علي وابن عباس أن اسمه عبد الله بن الضحاك

rows.speaker: محمد بن علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: A report from Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn gives the name Ayyash.
rows.anchor: وعن محمد بن علي بن الحسين عياش

rows.speaker: أبو خيثمة، علي
rows.claim: Abu Khaythama identifies him as al-Sa'b ibn Jabir ibn al-Qalamus, while another report calls him Marzuban ibn Marzuba the Greek; Ali says he descended from Japheth's first generation.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي خيثمة هو الصعب بن جابر بن القلمس. وقيل: مرزبان بن مرزبة اليوناني

rows.speaker: الحسن، وهب
rows.claim: Hasan says Dhū al-Qarnayn came after Thamud and lived 1,600 years; Wahb places him in the interval between Jesus and Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن: كان بعد ثمود وكان عمره ألف سنة وستمائة. وعن وهب: كان في الفترة بين عيسى ومحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address “upon you” is directed to the questioners, whether Jews or Quraysh; “a reminder” can mean the Qur'an or a report and good counsel.
rows.anchor: والخطاب في عليكم للسائلين إما اليهود وإما قريش على الخلاف الذي سبق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His empowerment means that he ruled the world and all kings submitted to him; other interpreters say it was prophetic authority and miracles, command of clouds and light, or abundant forces, awe, and ease of travel.
rows.anchor: والتمكين الذي له في الأرض كونه ملك الدنيا ودانت له الملوك كلها

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين، author
rows.claim: Some exegetes argue Dhū al-Qarnayn must be Alexander because he reached the inhabited world's west, east, and northern limit near Gog and Magog; such an extraordinary empire should be remembered, and history records only Alexander attaining it. The author concludes this proves Alexander, son of Philip.
rows.anchor: والملك الذي اسمه في كتب التواريخ أنه بلغ ملكه إلى هذا الحد ليس إلا الإسكندر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says four people ruled the earth, two believers: Solomon son of David and Dhū al-Qarnayn.
rows.anchor: في الحديث: «إن الذين ملكوا الأرض أربعة مؤمنان: سليمان بن داود، وذو القرنين»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views explain his empowerment as prophethood and miracles, a cloud that carried him with light making day and night equal, or numerous helpers, armies, fear in enemies, and knowledge of roads, land, and sea.
rows.anchor: وقيل تمكينه في الأرض بالنبوة وإجراء المعجزات. وقيل: تمكينه بأن سخر له السحاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sabab is whatever enables the desired goal: a route, knowledge, ability, or tool; the word originally meant a rope and broadened to anything by which one reaches an aim. Hasan glosses it as reaching wherever he wished.
rows.anchor: والسبب ما يتوصل به إني المقصود من علم أو قدرة أو آلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings with a light or doubled t in fa-atbaʿa are apparently synonymous; Yunus ibn Habib and Abu Zayd distinguish them, with hamza-cut form implying urgent, vigorous pursuit and connected hamza only following.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنهما بمعنى واحد. وعن يونس بن حبيب وأبي زيد أنه بقطع الهمزة عبارة عن المجد المسرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readers say the sun sets at a hot spring, others at a muddy spring; both descriptions can apply together. Abu Hatim allows hamiyah to mean a spring with mud through softened hamza; the Torah says water and mud.
rows.anchor: ولا تنافي بين الحامية والحمئة إذ تكون العين جامعة للوصفين

rows.speaker: تبع
rows.claim: Tubba's verse describes the sun setting in a spring of water, mud, and black matter, witnessing the muddy-spring reading.
rows.anchor: فرأى مغيب الشمس عند مآبها ... في عين ذي خلب وثاط حرمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Abu Dharr report, the Prophet says the sun sets in a hot spring. The author takes “in a spring” as the verse's apparent syntax, rejects evasive readings that make it only an appearance, and allows the spring to be in the sea or the sun to set behind it; some Baghdadis take “in” as “near.”
rows.anchor: وهذا الحديث وظاهر النص دليل على أن قوله في عين متعلق بقوله تغرب

rows.speaker: ابن السائب، وهب، أبو زيد السهيلي
rows.claim: Reports variously describe the people near the spring as believers and unbelievers, savage unbelievers who ate sun-scorched animals and fish, or people of Habus/Jerjisa descended from Thamud; Wahb narrates Dhū al-Qarnayn gathered and invited them, with some accepting and some refusing.
rows.anchor: قال ابن السائب: مؤمنين وكافرين. وقال غيره: كفرة لباسهم جلود السباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We said” most plausibly means God revealed through an angel; another view has direct speech to Dhū al-Qarnayn, making him a prophet. The author rejects mere inspiration as inadequate grounds for legal duties and taking lives.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله قلنا أنه أوحى الله إليه على لسان ملك

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Ali ibn Isa says the phrase means Muhammad said “they said, O Dhū al-Qarnayn”; the omitted first saying is removed because Dhū al-Qarnayn was not established as a prophet, and “they” means his troops.
rows.anchor: المعنى قلنا يا محمد قالوا يا ذا القرنين ثم حذف القول الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The choice is either to punish by killing for unbelief or to treat people well by urging faith and guidance; naming the consequence stands for its cause.
rows.anchor: إما أن تكفر فتعذب، وإما أن تؤمن فتحسن فعبر في التخيير بالمسبب عن السبب

rows.speaker: الطبري، author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says kindness means taking them captive while they remain unbelievers. The author rejects this because Dhū al-Qarnayn distinguishes wrongdoers from believers and chooses invitation and effort to win them over; persistent unbelievers face punishment in both worlds, while believers receive the good reward.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: اتخاذ الحسن هو أسرهم مع كفرهم يعني أنه خير مع كفرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future tense in “we will punish him” allows time for an invitation to faith and refusal; Dhū al-Qarnayn does not kill for wrongdoing immediately.
rows.anchor: وأتى بحرف التنفيس في فسوف نعذبه لما يتخلل بين إظهاره كفره وبين تعذيبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then he returns to his Lord” means on Judgment Day; the first-person plural in “we punish him” follows royal convention. The wording may suggest the choice was not God's, though it could be God's choice relayed by Dhū al-Qarnayn to his followers.
rows.anchor: وقوله ثم يرد إلى ربه أي يوم القيامة وأتى بنون العظمة في نعذبه على عادة الملوك في قولهم نحن فعلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence first names immediate, perceptible punishment and then God's final punishment; for believers it first names Paradise, their hoped-for hereafter reward, then gentle worldly speech.
rows.anchor: بدأ بما هو أقرب لهم ومحسوس عندهم، وهو قوله فسوف نعذبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-husna means Paradise; Dhū al-Qarnayn says only that he will speak gently, stopping short of promising acts of kindness out of deference to God, though kindness is understood.
rows.anchor: الحسنى أي الجنة لأن طمع المؤمن في الآخرة ورجاءه هو الذي حمله

rows.speaker: حمزة، الكسائي، حفص، أبو بحرية وآخرون
rows.claim: These readers recite jazāʾan with accusative and nunation, parsed as a circumstantial verbal noun meaning “rewarded,” as a cognate accusative, or, per al-Farra, a specification; al-Hasan says such fronting is rare except in poetry.
rows.anchor: فله جزاء بالنصب والتنوين وانتصب جزاء على أنه مصدر في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة، أبو علي
rows.claim: The remaining canonical readers recite jazāʾu al-husnā with nominative construct; it can mean reward for good deeds, or take al-husna as the good reward itself, Paradise, in an attributive/genitive construction.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة جزاء الحسنى برفع جزاء مضافا إلى الحسنى

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي إسحاق، ابن عباس، مسروق
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Ishaq reads jazāʾu nominative as a subject with al-husna in apposition; Ibn Abbas and Masruq read accusative without nunation, with an implied “reward” or deleted tanwin; Abu Jaʿfar reads yusran with a damma on its sīn wherever it occurs.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله بن أبي إسحاق فله جزاء مرفوع وهو مبتدأ وخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhū al-Qarnayn next followed a route toward his appointed destination.
rows.anchor: ثم أتبع سببا أي طريقا إلى مقصده الذي يسر له

rows.speaker: الحسن، عيسى، ابن محيصن، ابن كثير
rows.claim: Some read maṭliʿ with an open lām, the analogical form, also reported from Ibn Kathir and Meccans; most read with kasra, a transmitted form in limited cases, although its analogy would have a kasra in the imperfect.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وعيسى وابن محيصن مطلع بفتح اللام

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisai says the kasra form is a dialect that has died out in most Arabic; the sentence continues that people no longer say taṭluʿ with kasra.
rows.anchor: وكان الكسائي يقول: هذه لغة ماتت في كثير من لغات العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We gave them no screen from it” is explained by comparison with the western people whom Dhū al-Qarnayn also found unbelieving; their judgment likewise distinguishes unbelievers to punish from believers to treat well.
rows.anchor: لم نجعل لهم من دونها سترا كذلك أي مثل أولئك الذين وجدهم في مغرب الشمس كفرة مثلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading compares their lack of a screen to the many kinds of shelter God gave the addressees: mountains, forts, buildings, alcoves, and clothes.
rows.anchor: وقيل لم نجعل لهم من دونها سترا مثل ذلك الستر الذي جعلنا لكم من الجبال والحصون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes “likewise” to describe Dhū al-Qarnayn's affairs as narrated, magnifying his achievement.
rows.anchor: كذلك أي أمر ذي القرنين كذلك أي كما وصفناه تعظيما لأمره

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya's first explanation is that Dhū al-Qarnayn acted toward the sunrise people as he had toward the western people, while the wording also reports God's encompassing knowledge of his actions.
rows.anchor: كذلك معناه فعل معهم كفعله مع الأولين أهل المغرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation says their situation paralleled the western people: they were unbelievers too and were treated according to the same distinction between disbelief and faith.
rows.anchor: وحكمهم مثل حكمهم في التعذيب لمن بقي على الكفر والإحسان لمن آمن

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya allows “likewise” to begin a new statement about God's encompassing knowledge of Dhū al-Qarnayn's deeds, but says the preceding parallel interpretation is sounder; an independent reading needs an implied predicate.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون كذلك استئناف قول ولا يكون راجعا على الطائفة الأولى

rows.speaker: وهب، الهروي
rows.claim: On the northern route, Wahb places the two high mountains at the edge of Turk lands near Armenia and Azerbaijan; al-Harawi says they lie beyond Turk territory.
rows.anchor: وهما بمنقطع أرض الترك مما يلي أرمينية وأذربيجان. وذكر الهروي أنهما جبلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts describe two smooth, slippery northern mountains; each is a barrier to the earth's passes, with an opening between them through which Gog and Magog entered.
rows.anchor: هما جبلان من جهة الشمال لينان أملسان، يزلق عليهما كل شيء

rows.speaker: مجاهد، عكرمة، النخعي، حفص، ابن كثير، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers pronounce the sīn of al-saddayn open; the rest of the Seven pronounce it rounded. Al-Kisai calls them two dialects with one meaning, while al-Khalil and Sibawayh distinguish the rounded noun from the open verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وعكرمة والنخعي وحفص وابن كثير وأبو عمرو بين السدين بفتح السين

rows.speaker: عكرمة، أبو عمرو بن العلاء، أبو عبيدة، ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: They distinguish the vowels by origin or visibility: God's creation takes damma and human construction fatha; Ibn Abi Ishaq says what the eye sees takes damma and unseen things fatha.
rows.anchor: ما كان من خلق الله لم يشارك فيه أحد فهو بالضم، وما كان من صنع البشر فبالفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word bayna is accusative as the object of “reached”; in general bayna is a flexible adverb unless compounded with another like word.
rows.anchor: وانتصب بين على أنه مفعول به يبلغ

rows.speaker: الزمخشري، author
rows.claim: The people were human beings, whom al-Zamakhshari identifies as Turks; calling them jinn is far-fetched. Their land was at the Turk frontier toward the east.
rows.anchor: وقوما يعني من البشر. وقال الزمخشري: هم الترك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري، author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes “they could hardly understand speech” to imply eventual understanding after difficulty, reflecting the claim that negating yakādu affirms its action; the author says this is not the preferred analysis.
rows.anchor: لا يكادون يفهمونه إلا بجهد ومشقة كأنه فهم من نفي يكاد أنه يقع منهم الفهم

rows.speaker: الأعمش، ابن أبي ليلى، خلف، ابن عيسى الأصبهاني، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: These readers pronounce yufqihūn with passive-like vowels, meaning they make their speech understood by listeners; their unfamiliar language is unclear to outsiders.
rows.anchor: يفقهون بضم الياء وكسر القاف أي يفهمون السامع كلامهم

rows.speaker: author، السدي، الضحاك، قتادة
rows.claim: Gog and Magog are two tribes descended from Adam, or from Japheth; views identify them as Turks and Jil/Dailam. Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak say a small Turk remnant escaped and raided; Qatada and al-Suddi say the barrier blocked 21 tribes while one Turk tribe remained outside. Their number and traits lack sound reports.
rows.anchor: ويأجوج ومأجوج من ولد آدم قبيلتان. وقيل: هما من ولد يافث بن نوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj are diptotes: if foreign, because of foreignness and proper-name status; if Arabic tribal names, because of femininity and proper-name status.
rows.anchor: وهما ممنوعا الصرف، فمن زعم أنهما أعجميان فللعجمة والعلمية

rows.speaker: الأخفش، قطرب، السخاوي
rows.claim: Grammarians offer different roots and patterns for the names: al-Akhfash derives them from fire's crackle or Arabic verbs, Qutrub gives alternative patterns, and al-Sakhawi thinks they are Arabic forms originally written with hamza.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: إن جعلنا ألفهما أصلية فيأجوج يفعول ومأجوج مفعول

rows.speaker: علي بن عبد الصمد السخاوي
rows.claim: Al-Sakhawi derives them from agitation and surging, rapid running, intense heat, or bitter salty water; he cites a poet's line and the verse about their surging and descending from every height.
rows.anchor: إما من الأجة وهو الاختلاف كما قال تعالى وتركنا بعضهم يومئذ يموج

rows.speaker: عاصم، الأعمش، يعقوب، الفراء
rows.claim: These readers use hamza in Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj, also known in Banu Asad; the author says the only cited rationale is an unusual dialect reported of al-ʿAjjaj, who hamzated words such as “world” and “ring.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم والأعمش ويعقوب في رواية بالهمز وفي يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة، العجاج، رؤبة
rows.claim: The rest of the Seven use unhamzated forms, the language of Arabs other than Banu Asad; al-ʿAjjaj and his son Ruʾba instead say Ājūj with hamza replacing yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة بألف غير مهموزة وهي لغة كل العرب غير بني أسد

rows.speaker: سعيد بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: The wording says their corruption actually occurred, rather than being merely feared, since the people complained of harm; Saʿid ibn Abd al-Aziz says it was their eating human beings.
rows.anchor: وإفسادهم الظاهر تحقق الإفساد منهم لا توقعه لأنها شكت من ضررنا لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views call their corruption oppression, murder, and ordinary human mischief, or say they ate every green thing and carried off every dry thing in spring; an extraordinary report says none died before seeing a thousand armed sons.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو الظلم والقتل ووجوه الإفساد المعلوم من البشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people politely offer payment to secure help with the barrier, like Moses asking Khidr permission to follow him.
rows.anchor: استدعاء منهم قبول ما يبذلونه مما يعينه على ما طلبوا على جهة حسن الأدب

rows.speaker: الحسن، الأعمش، طلحة، خلف، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: These readers use kharājan with long ā here, while others read kharjan; both forms mean payment or money raised for the barrier, though lexicographers distinguish the terms by scope, source, or recurrence.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والأعمش وطلحة وخلف وابن سعدان وابن عيسى الأصبهاني وابن جبير الأنطاكي ومن السبعة حمزة والكسائي خراجا بألف هنا

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي، ثعلب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says kharj is levied on heads and kharaj on land; Thaʿlab calls kharj narrower and kharaj broader. Some distinguish a one-time payment from recurring revenue.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: الخرج على الرؤوس يقال: أد خرج رأسك، والخراج على الأرض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses kharājan as wages.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس خراجا أجرا

rows.speaker: نافع، ابن عامر، أبو بكر
rows.claim: These readers pronounce the sīn of sadd with damma; several other named readers and the remainder of the Seven use fatha.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر سدا بضم السين

rows.speaker: author، مقاتل، الكلبي
rows.claim: Dhū al-Qarnayn says God's grant of power and dominion is better than their payment; he asks for strong workers and skilled builders, per Muqatil, or tools, per al-Kalbi, and calls for a fortified barrier.
rows.anchor: ما بسط الله لي من القدرة والملك خير من خرجكم فأعينوني بقوة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، حميد، باقي السبعة
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Humayd read mākkanan with two moving nūns; the rest of the Seven assimilate the nun of makkan into the protective nun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وحميد: ما مكنني بنونين متحركتين

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says “bring me iron blocks” requests that the materials be handed over, not donated, since Dhū al-Qarnayn already refused their payment; Abu Bakr reads the verb “come to me,” and the syntax implies a preposition.
rows.anchor: إنما هو استدعاء مناولة لا استدعاء عطية وهبة لأنه قد ارتبط من قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers open the bāʾ in zubar; Hasan rounds it. A suppressed phrase means the people brought the iron blocks, and Dhū al-Qarnayn ordered them stacked until the two sides were level.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور زبر بفتح الباء والحسن بضمها، وفي الكلام حذف تقديره فأتوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports describe digging the foundation to water, filling it with stone and clay and molten copper, placing iron between wood and charcoal, heating it with bellows, then pouring copper over it to fuse it into a solid mountain.
rows.anchor: ثم جعل حشوه الصخر وطينه النحاس مذاب، ثم يصب عليه والبنيان من زبر الحديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account gives the barrier's length as one hundred farsakhs and its width as fifty.
rows.anchor: وقيل: طول ما بين السدين مائة فرسخ وعرضه خمسون

rows.speaker: رجل
rows.claim: A man who told the Prophet what the barrier looked like said it resembled a patterned cloak with black and red stripes; the Prophet replied that he had seen it.
rows.anchor: أن رجلا أخبر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم به فقال

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر، أبو بكر، ابن محيصن وآخرون
rows.claim: The readers give several vowel patterns for al-ṣadafayn, with forms rounding or opening ṣād and dāl, and sometimes pausing the dāl; the passage also omits an implied “they blew” before the iron became fire.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والزهري ومجاهد والحسن الصدفين بضم الصاد والدال

rows.speaker: الأعمش، طلحة، حمزة، أبو بكر
rows.claim: Some readers say “bring me” with a verb of coming rather than giving; qiṭr is molten copper, governed by “pour,” while an object of “bring” is omitted because the following phrase supplies it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش وطلحة وحمزة وأبو بكر بخلاف عنه قال: ائتوني أي جيئوني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gog and Magog could neither climb the barrier because it was high, distant, and smooth, nor pierce it because it was thick and hard; these are the only two ways to pass it.
rows.anchor: أن يظهروه أي يصلوا عليه لبعده وارتفاعه واملاسه، ولا أن ينقبوه لصلابته وثخانته

rows.speaker: حمزة، طلحة، أبو علي، الأعمش
rows.claim: Most readers drop the first tāʾ from istāʿū for ease near ṭāʾ; Hamza and Talha assimilate it, though Abu Ali calls that invalid. Other readings replace sīn with ṣād or retain the tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور فما اسطاعوا بحذف التاء تخفيفا لقربها من الطاء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية، الزمخشري
rows.claim: “This is mercy from my Lord” is spoken by Dhū al-Qarnayn; Ibn Atiyya points to the barrier, its strength, and its benefit, while al-Zamakhshari points to the barrier or the God-given ability to build it.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: إشارة إلى السد أي هذا السد نعمة من الله ورحمة على عباده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view supplies an omitted clause: when the barrier was complete, level, and firm, Dhū al-Qarnayn called it a mercy from his Lord; another reader makes the demonstrative feminine.
rows.anchor: قيل: وفي الكلام حذف وتقديره فلما أكمل بناء السد واستوى واستحكم

rows.speaker: author، الزمخشري
rows.claim: The promise may mean Judgment Day or Gog and Magog's emergence; al-Zamakhshari chooses the approach of Judgment Day, when the barrier is made flat and crushed to earth.
rows.anchor: والوعد يحتمل أن يراد به يوم القيامة، وأن يراد به وقت خروج يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading dakkan is a verbal noun with tanwin; the Kufans read dakkā, long and indeclinable. The barrier becomes another form rather than being created anew, and waʿd here means the promised event, not a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وهذا بعيد جدا لأن السد إذ ذاك موجود مخلوق ولا يخلق المخلوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes “some of them” as all creatures on the day God's promise arrives, i.e. Judgment Day, supported by the following blowing of the trumpet, gathering, and presentation of Hell; the trumpet was discussed in al-Anʿam.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الضمير في بعضهم يعود على الخلق أي يوم إذ جاء وعد الله وهو يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jamʿan is a verbal noun like mawʿid; “we exposed Hell” means we displayed it on the day of gathering. The lām can mean “upon,” as in a poem; the reversed construction is far-fetched, and singling out unbelievers reassures believers.
rows.anchor: وجمعا مصدر كموعد وعرضنا أي أبرزنا جهنم يومئذ أي يوم إذ جمعناهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of a veil over the eyes is a metaphor for failing to see God's signs and take heed; “from my remembrance” can mean from Quranic reflection, with an omitted genitive, and eyes means insight, not physical organs.
rows.anchor: والمراد أنهم لا يبصرون آياتي التي ينظر إليها فيعتبر بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They could not hear” intensifies the absence of hearing: even a deaf person may hear a shout, but these people's ears are so closed that they cannot hear at all.
rows.anchor: وكانوا لا يستطيعون سمعا مبالغة في انتفاء السمع إذ نفيت الاستطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke targets people who worship angels, Ezra, Christ, or idols, including some Arabs, Jews, and Christians; taking them as allies will bring no benefit. “God's servants” may mean devils per Ibn Abbas or idols per Muqatil, but the author prefers creatures as an honorific possessive.
rows.anchor: والأظهر تفسير العباد بما قلناه لإضافتهم إليه والأكثر أن تكون الإضافة في مثل هذا اللفظ إضافة تشريف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hasiba means “suppose”; Abdullah's reading afazanna makes that meaning explicit.
rows.anchor: وحسب هنا بمعنى ظن وبه قرأ عبد الله أفظن

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب، زيد بن علي، مجاهد، قتادة وآخرون
rows.claim: A long list of readers recites afahasb with a still sīn and nominative bāʾ, construing hasb as sufficiency or limit in relation to the following clause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي بن أبي طالب وزيد بن علي بن الحسين ويحيى بن يعمر ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author، سهل
rows.claim: The reading afahasb is parsed as a subject whose predicate is “that they take My servants as allies”; Sahl glosses it as their sufficiency and utmost expectation, which intensifies the blame.
rows.anchor: مضافا إلى الذين أي أفكافيهم ومحسبهم ومنتهى عرضهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري، author، سيبويه
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari parses hasb as a governing participle under the interrogative; the author objects that hasb is not a participle, though he allows that similar noun-like descriptions may govern a following subject, citing Sibawayh.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن هذا الإعراب لا يجوز لأن حسبا ليس باسم فاعل فتعمل

rows.speaker: الزجاج، القتبي
rows.claim: Nuzul can mean the place where one alights, per al-Zajjaj, or food prepared for a guest, per al-Qutaybi; it may also be a collective of nāzil and a circumstantial accusative.
rows.anchor: والنزل هنا يحتمل التفسيرين وكونه موضع النزول قاله الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author compares nuzul as food prepared for a guest to the promise of painful punishment and cites poetry; Abu Haywa and one transmission from Abu Amr read nuzlan with a still zāy.
rows.anchor: وقيل: جمع نازل ونصبه على الحال نحو شارف وشرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad is told to ask the unbelievers whether he should inform them of the greatest losers in deeds; once they ask for the answer, he should identify those who disbelieved.
rows.anchor: أي قل يا محمد للكافرين هل نخبركم الآية فإذا طلبوا ذلك فقل لهم أولئك الذين كفروا

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali identifies the greatest losers as monks, by analogy with the “toiling, weary” phrase.
rows.anchor: عن علي هم الرهبان كقوله عاملة ناصبة

rows.speaker: مجاهد، author
rows.claim: Mujahid says the People of the Book; other views say the Sabians or, in Ali's answer to Ibn al-Kawwa, the Harurites. The author treats these as examples, not an exhaustive definition: the label covers those outside Islam, show-offs, and heretics whose innovations lead to unbelief.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد: هم أهل الكتاب. وقيل: هم الصابئون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worst loser is one whose effort exhausts him yet leads him to the Fire; aʿmālan is an accusative specification because their misguided deeds differ.
rows.anchor: والأخسر من أتعب نفسه فأدى تعبه به إلى النار. وانتصب أعمالا على التمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alladhīna may be nominative as the predicate of an omitted “they are,” or accusative for censure; the next clause can then be its description or apposition.
rows.anchor: والذين يصح رفعه على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف، أي هم الذين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍalla saʿyuhum means their effort perished, became void, and vanished. Yaḥsabūn and yuḥsinūn differ only by dots, an example of tajnīs al-taṣḥīf.
rows.anchor: ضل سعيهم أي هلك وبطل وذهب ويحسبون ويحسنون من تجنيس التصحيف

rows.speaker: البحتري، شاعر مجهول
rows.claim: Al-Buhturi's line illustrates the dot-based wordplay; another poem is given in a deliberately mispointed form, then restored as “you watered me, my Lord …,” for the same unusual pun.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول أبي عبادة البحتري: ولم يكن المغتر بالله إذ سرى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، أبو السمال
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Abu al-Sammal read ḥabiṭat with an open bāʾ; the majority read it with kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس وأبو السمال فحبطت بفتح الباء والجمهور بكسرها

rows.speaker: مجاهد، عبيد بن عمير، ابن محيصن، يعقوب
rows.claim: The majority read “we do not establish a weight” with first-person plural and accusative wazana; other readings use third-person singular or intransitive yaqumu, with wazan as its subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور فلا نقيم بالنون وزنا بالنصب ومجاهد وعبيد بن عمير فلا يقيم بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not establishing a weight may mean the losers have no good deeds to weigh and therefore enter the Fire, or figuratively that they have no worth with God.
rows.anchor: واحتمل قوله فلا نقيم إلا به أنهم لا حسنة لهم توزن في موازين القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two reports illustrate the verse: a glutton, drinker, and tall man will not weigh even a mosquito's wing; other people bring deeds as large as Tihama mountains that weigh nothing.
rows.anchor: يؤتى بالأكول الشروب الطويل فلا يزن جناح بعوضة

rows.speaker: author، أبو البقاء
rows.claim: “That is their recompense” may point to denying them weight, with Hell as apposition; several alternative sentence analyses are listed, but attaching the causal bāʾ to jazāʾuhum is disallowed because of the intervening words.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن تتعلق الباء بجزاؤهم للفصل بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's signs here are the miracles shown through prophets and the revealed scriptures given to them.
rows.anchor: والآيات هي المعجزات الظاهرة على أيدي الأنبياء والصحف الإلهية المنزلة عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing what is prepared for unbelievers, God describes what is prepared for believers in the Gardens of Firdaws.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر تعالى ما أعد للكافرين ذكر ما أعد للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report in the Ṣaḥīḥ describes the Gardens of Firdaws as four gardens: two with gold ornaments, vessels, and contents, and two with silver.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحيح جنات الفردوس أربع ثنتان من ذهب حليتهما وآنيتهما وما فيهما

rows.speaker: عبادة
rows.claim: A hadith from Ubada calls Firdaws the highest part of Paradise.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث عبادة الفردوس أعلاها يعني أعلا الجنة

rows.speaker: عبادة، قتادة
rows.claim: Ubada calls Firdaws the highest part of Paradise, and Qatada says it is the high hillock from which the rivers of Paradise flow.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث عبادة الفردوس أعلاها يعني أعلا الجنة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra describes Firdaws as a mountain from which the rivers of Paradise burst forth.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو هريرة جبل تتفجر منه أنهار الجنة

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: A hadith from Abu Umama calls Firdaws the navel of Paradise.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أبي أمامة الفردوس سرة الجنة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Firdaws means garden in the Roman language.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد الفردوس البستان بالرومية

rows.speaker: كعب، الضحاك، عبيد الله بن الحارث بن كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb and al-Dahhak identify Firdaws as grape gardens; Ubayd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Kaʿb narrows it to gardens of vines and grapes among fruits.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب والضحاك جنات الفردوس الأعناب

rows.speaker: المبرد، الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says Arabic firdaws means dense trees, especially grapes; al-Zajjaj says it is a valley growing varied plants. Scholars dispute whether the word is Arabic or Persian, Roman, or Syriac.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: الفردوس فيما سمعت من كلام العرب الشجر الملتف والأغلب عليه العنب

rows.speaker: حسان، أمية بن أبي الصلت
rows.claim: Hassan uses firdaws in a poem; the claim that his is the only Arabic occurrence is refuted by a verse from Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. Farādīs is the plural of firdaws.
rows.anchor: قيل: ولم يسمع بالفردوس في كلام العرب إلا في هذا البيت بيت حسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of “Gardens of Firdaws” is gardens around or associated with Firdaws, hence the genitive construction.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن معنى جنات الفردوس بساتين حول الفردوس ولذلك أضاف الجنات إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A trellised vineyard is called karm mufardas; a palm grove below Yamama and Damascus's Bab al-Faradis also take the name from their dense, trained planting.
rows.anchor: ويقال: كرم مفردس أي معرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuzulan has the same range of interpretation as earlier; ḥawlan means being moved elsewhere, and Ibn Isa calls it a verbal noun like ʿiwaj and ṣighar.
rows.anchor: ونزلا يحتمل من التأويل ما احتمل قوله نزلا المتقدم. ومعنى حولا أي محولا إلى غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted verb is understood from the sense: the sea would be exhausted before the Lord's words were exhausted.
rows.anchor: محذوف لدلالة المعنى عليه تقديره لنفد

rows.speaker: الأعرج
rows.claim: The majority read madadan with both vowels open and no alif; al-Aʿraj reads the mīm with kasra, parsing it as a specification after mithl.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور بمثله مددا بفتح الميم والدال بغير ألف، والأعرج بكسر الميم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود، ابن عباس، مجاهد، الأعمش وآخرون
rows.claim: These readers recite madādan with an alif and kasra on the mīm; al-Razi allows it as a verbal noun meaning “were we to replenish it, a replenishing,” with madd standing for imdād.
rows.anchor: بمثله مدادا بألف بين الدالين وكسر الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling himself a human like the audience affirms shared humanity, not angelhood; his distinction is that revelation comes to him. Mention of one God counters idol worship and leads into the means of salvation.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله بشر مثلكم إعلام بالبشرية والمماثلة في ذلك لا أدعي أني ملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yarjū means to hope; meeting the Lord implies an omitted good or reward. A second view takes it as fearing a bad encounter, but hope better fits the encouragement to expect God's generosity.
rows.anchor: وحمل الرجاء على بابه أجود لبسط النفس إلى إحسان الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr explains not associating anyone in worship as refusing showiness and seeking only God's face without mixing another aim into the deed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير: لا يرائي في عمله فلا يبتغي إلا وجه ربه خالصا

rows.speaker: جندب بن زهير
rows.claim: Jundub ibn Zuhayr said he worked for God but felt pleased when people saw him; the Prophet replied that God does not accept an act shared with another.
rows.anchor: نزلت في جندب بن زهير قال لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: إني أعمل العمل لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report promises two rewards, for private work and public work, when the person intends to be an example; Muawiya says this was the last verse revealed.
rows.anchor: لك أجران أجر السر وأجر العلانية

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Most read “and does not associate” in the third person; Abu Amr's transmission uses second person, then the text returns to third person with rabbihi to keep both pronouns aligned with “whoever.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو في رواية الجعفي عنه: ولا تشرك بالتاء خطابا للسامع

none: This segment consists of Qur'an text reciting 19:66-98, including 19:96, without commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to remember Abraham follows the account of Mary and Jesus: after explaining how groups wrongly worshiped them, the text recalls Abraham's rejection of idols as a reminder to Arabs of his monotheism and as evidence that Muhammad receives revelation truthfully.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة هذه الآية لما قبلها أنه تعالى لما ذكر قصة مريم وابنها عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣiddīq is an intensive form from truthfulness: Abraham was consistently truthful in speech and deeds, and ṣidq can describe character and even objects, as in good measure of food or solid timber.
rows.anchor: والصديق من أبنية المبالغة وهو مبني من الثلاثي للمبالغة أي كثير الصدق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truthfulness can describe deeds, character, and inanimate things; expressions such as ṣadaqan for a measured quantity and ʿūd ṣidq for sound timber show the word's breadth.
rows.anchor: يقال: صدقني الطعام كذا وكذا قفيزا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣiddīqiyya has ranks; the author notes as an unusual grammatical opinion that intensive forms derived from transitive verbs can govern an object, as in “one who drinks intoxicants.”
rows.anchor: والصديقية مراتب ألا ترى إلى وصف المؤمنين بها في قوله من النبيين والصديقين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Abraham's truthfulness was exceptional in believing God's unseen signs, books, messengers, and especially the scriptures and prophets; Abraham was also a prophet and a forceful witness to truth.
rows.anchor: والمراد فرط صدقه وكثرة ما صدق به من غيوب الله وآياته وكتبه ورسوله

rows.speaker: author، الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats “when he said to his father” as parenthetic or links it to kāna or ṣiddīqan nabiyyan; the author challenges the syntax, noting disputes over whether ʾidh declines and whether defective kāna governs adverbs.
rows.anchor: فالتخريج الأول يقتضي تصرف إذ وقد تقدم لنا أنها لا تتصرف

rows.speaker: أبو البر هثيم
rows.claim: Abu al-Barr al-Haytham reads innahu kāna ṣādiqan, “he was truthful,” instead of ṣiddīqan.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو البر هثيم إنه كان صادقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing his father as yā abati is a tactful appeal through their kinship.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله يا أبت تلطف واستدعاء بالنسب

rows.speaker: ابن عامر، الأعرج، أبو جعفر، هارون
rows.claim: Some read yā abati with an open tāʾ, which Harun criticized; the reading was discussed in Surat Yusuf. Abd Allah's codex has wā abati, with wāw instead of yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر والأعرج وأبو جعفر يا أبت بفتح التاء وقد لحن هارون هذه القراءة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari praises Abraham's gentle sequence and considerate language in advising a father deeply mistaken in idol worship, emphasizing courtesy, kindness, and good character.
rows.anchor: كيف رتب الكلام معه في أحسن اتساق وساقه أرشق مساق مع استعمال المجاملة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra transmits a report that God told Abraham to keep good character even with unbelievers; al-Zamakhshari adds extensive exhortatory material that the author omits.
rows.anchor: حدث أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā lā yasmaʿ is likely a relative clause, though it can be an indefinite noun with description; the point is that idols lack hearing and sight without specifying an object. Shayʾan may be a verbal noun or object.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنها موصولة، وجوزوا أن تكون نكرة موصوفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham does not call his father ignorant; instead, because the father cannot explain idol worship, Abraham says he has received some knowledge the father lacks. The exchange suggests Abraham had already become a prophet.
rows.anchor: وهذه المحاورة تدل على أن ذلك كان بعد ما نبىء، إذ في لفظ جاءني تجدد العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The knowledge Abraham received is variously explained as revelation brought by an angel, knowledge of the afterlife and its recompense, or knowledge of God's oneness and exclusive right to worship.
rows.anchor: والذي جاءه الوحي الذي أتى به الملك أو العلم بأمور الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Follow me” means follow Abraham in worshiping one God; the straight path is faith and exclusive worship of God.
rows.anchor: فاتبعني على توحيد الله بالعبادة وارفض الأصنام يهديك صراطا مستقيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Serving Satan means obeying him in idol worship; Satan disobeyed the Merciful by refusing to prostrate to Adam and is an enemy of both the father and Adam.
rows.anchor: وعبادته كونه يطيعه في عبادة الأصنام ثم نفره عن عبادة الشيطان بأنه كان عصيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God al-Raḥmān highlights the breadth of His mercy and why He alone deserves worship; Satan was expelled from that mercy, chose rebellion, and seeks disobedience for Adam's descendants too.
rows.anchor: وكان لفظ الرحمن هنا تنبيها على سعة رحمته، وأن من هذا وصفه هو الذي ينبغي أن يعبد

rows.speaker: الفراء، الطبري، author
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Tabari take akhāfu as “I know,” like “we feared they would overwhelm them”; the author prefers its ordinary sense because Abraham still hoped his father would believe and feared his persistence in disbelief.
rows.anchor: والأولى حمل أخاف على موضوعه الأصلي لأنه لم يكن آيسا من إيمانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's gentle rhetoric says “touch” instead of punish, leaves the torment indefinite, and presents Satan's patronage as an even worse result; he begins each appeal with “my father” to soften it.
rows.anchor: وخوفه إبراهيم سوء العاقبة وتأدب معه إذ لم يصرح بلحوق العذاب به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes Satan's patronage companionship in the afterlife even if the two hate and disown each other; another reverses the order, making the father Satan's ally in this world and the torment later.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الولاية هنا كونه مقرونا معه في الآخرة وإن تباغضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened touch of punishment need not be in the afterlife: it may mean divine abandonment that turns the father toward Satan, or a worldly punishment that makes him persist in disbelief until death.
rows.anchor: بل يحتمل أن يحمل العذاب على الخذلان من الله فيصير مواليا للشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's continued appeals show intense concern to guide his father, fulfilling filial duty and steering him toward guidance; a hadith says guiding one man through you is better than red camels.
rows.anchor: وهذه المناصحات تدل على شدة تعلق قلبه بمعالجة أبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father asks in a rebuking, denying tone whether Abraham is turning away from his idols; “desire away from” means deliberate rejection. He calls him by name, not “my son,” and speaks harshly.
rows.anchor: استفهم استفهام إنكار، والرغبة عن الشيء تركه عمدا وآلهته أصنامه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the predicate comes before the subject in arāghib anta because it matters most to the father and conveys astonishment that anyone would abandon the idols; this consoles Muhammad about similar treatment by Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وقدم الخبر على المبتدأ في قوله أراغب أنت عن آلهتي لأنه كان أهم عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead parses rāghib as the subject, licensed by the interrogative, and anta as the agent filling the predicate slot; this avoids inversion and avoids separating rāghib from its complement with an unrelated word.
rows.anchor: والمختار في إعراب أراغب أنت أن يكون راغب مبتدأ لأنه قد اعتمد على أداة الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “stop” is omitted: the father may mean stop speaking to me this way and inviting me, or stop abandoning my idols; the threat answers an omitted oath.
rows.anchor: ومتعلق تنته محذوف واحتمل أن يكون عن مخاطبتي بما خاطبتني به

rows.speaker: الحسن، السدي، الضحاك، ابن جريج
rows.claim: They interpret lan arjumannaka as stoning, killing, or insulting, respectively.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: بالحجارة. وقيل: لأقتلنك. وقال السدي والضحاك وابن جريج

rows.speaker: الزمخشري، author، سيبويه
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted “beware of me” before “leave me” to make the coordination parallel; the author says no deletion is needed because Sibawayh permits a declarative and imperative clause to be coordinated.
rows.anchor: وإنما احتاج إلى حذف ليناسب بين جملتي العطف والمعطوف عليه

rows.speaker: الجمهور، الحسن، مجاهد، ابن جبير
rows.claim: Most readers and these authorities take miliyyan as an adverb meaning a long time; its cognates refer to night and day or a lengthy period, and a poet uses it for an extended stretch of youth.
rows.anchor: وانتصب مليا على الظرف أي دهرا طويلا قاله الجمهور والحسن ومجاهد وغيرهم

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh explains “walked upon him miliyyan” as meaning he stayed or traveled with him for a long time.
rows.anchor: وقال سيبويه: سير عليه ملي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others gloss miliyyan as being safe and sound, a circumstantial description of the person addressed; Ibn Atiyya paraphrases it as being self-sufficient and independent of the father.
rows.anchor: مليا معناه سالما سويا فهو حال من فاعل واهجرني

rows.speaker: السدي، ابن جبير
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says miliyyan means forever; Ibn Jubayr says a long time. The word's root conveys staying, as in tamallaytu ḥīnan.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: معناه أبدا. ومنه قول مهلهل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari offers another sense: leave me while still able to go, before I beat and disable you; maliyy means physically capable and strong enough for something.
rows.anchor: أو مليا بالذهاب عني والهجران قبل أن أثخنك بالضرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites Abraham saying “peace to you,” but says this prooftext is interpreted away and does not establish that one may initiate a greeting to unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم لأبيه سلام عليك وما استدل به متأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author parses nominative salāmun as a sentence and accusative salāman as a verbal noun, a prayer for safety and conciliatory address.
rows.anchor: ورفع سلام على الابتداء ونصبه على المصدر، أي سلمت سلاما دعاء له بالسلامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When ordered to leave for a long time, Abraham says he will obey and separate from his father, people, and idols; reports place his migration in Syria or Harran, where he married Sarah and met the ruler who gave Sarah Hajar.
rows.anchor: ولما أمره بهجره الزمان الطويل أخبره بأنه يتمثل أمره ويعتزله وقومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author counters permission to initiate greetings to unbelievers with the Sahih Muslim report forbidding greeting Jews and Christians first.
rows.anchor: لا تبدءوا اليهود والنصارى بالسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's promise to ask forgiveness presupposes a condition that makes forgiveness possible, namely belief; commands and prohibitions addressed to an unbeliever likewise can be fulfilled only upon belief.
rows.anchor: ثم وعده بالاستغفار وذلك يكون بشرط حصول ما يمكن معه الاستغفار وهو الإيمان بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I will ask forgiveness for you” means Abraham will pray for his father's guidance so that faith brings forgiveness; it does not mean he thought God forgives an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: ومعنى سأستغفر لك أدعو الله في هدايتك فيغفر لك بالإيمان

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya allows that Abraham may have been the first prophet taught that God does not forgive unbelief; the statement to his father would then precede that revelation, later resolved by the father's death in disbelief or a revealed final judgment.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون إبراهيم عليه السلام أول نبي أوحي إليه إن الله لا يغفر لكافر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري، author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari argues that reason alone does not forbid seeking forgiveness for an unbeliever before scriptural instruction; he cites Abraham's exception and rejects the claim that the father promised to believe, arguing Abraham was the promiser, as a reading by Hammad indicates.
rows.anchor: الذي يمنع من الاستغفار للكافر إنما هو السمع، فأما القضية العقلية فلا تأباه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، الكلبي، القتبي، السدي
rows.claim: Ḥafiyyan means honored, gracious, and full of kindness: Ibn Abbas says compassionate, al-Kalbi forbearing, al-Qutaybi devoted, and al-Suddi one who cares about your affair.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: رحيما. وقال الكلبي: حليما. وقال القتبي: بارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though Abraham's father was harsh, Abraham answered with peace and a promise to seek forgiveness out of filial duty.
rows.anchor: ولما كان في قوله لأرجمنك فظاظة وقساوة قلب قابله بالدعاء له بالسلام والأمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “I call upon my Lord,” the author understands calling as worship, in keeping with the parallel phrase “I worship my Lord.”
rows.anchor: والأظهر أن قوله وأدعوا ربي معناه وأعبد ربي
